lessons.title: Close-up: the mattress edge and the fan

zoom.label: The lower edge of the mattress, bottom right, with painted lettering

c1.text: Level one: Ingres painted her for the queen of Naples. Now zoom into the bottom right, along the edge of the mattress: there's writing.

zoom.label: The lower edge of the mattress, bottom right, with painted lettering

c1q.text: Where does Ingres's signature say he painted her?

sources.title: Musée du Louvre, collection record RF 1158, 'Une odalisque, dite La grande odalisque' (signature and history; our translations)
Henri Delaborde, Ingres, sa vie, ses travaux, sa doctrine (Paris, 1870), catalogue no. 75 (our translations)
Henry Lapauze, Ingres, sa vie et son œuvre (Paris, 1911) (our translations)

c1m.text: Ordered for Naples, signed in Rome in 1814, first shown in Paris in 1819.

c1a.text: Naples is where she was meant to go.

correction.tempting: Caroline Murat, queen of Naples, ordered the picture in 1813.
correction.truth: The signature ends 'Rom', for Rome, where Ingres worked. The picture never reached Naples.
correction.evidence: Louvre record: the signature at lower right. Delaborde (1870) and Lapauze (1911): it stayed on his hands in Rome.

c1b.text: Yes. The Louvre transcribes it 'J.A.Ingres. Pxit 1814.Rom': his name, the year 1814, and Rom, for Rome. You can read 'ROM' at the end.

c1c.text: Paris saw her first, but five years later.

correction.tempting: She was first shown in public at the Paris Salon of 1819.
correction.truth: The signature says 1814 and Rom, for Rome, where Ingres was then working.
correction.evidence: Louvre record: signature, and the Salon of 1819. Delaborde (1870): painted in 1814, shown in 1819.

zoom.label: Her right hand with gold bracelets, holding a fan of peacock feathers against her leg

c2.text: Level one: the title calls her an odalisque, a woman of a harem. Now zoom into her right hand, resting on her leg: a fan of peacock feathers.

zoom.label: Her right hand with gold bracelets, holding a fan of peacock feathers against her leg

c2q.text: What do props like this fan and her turban do?

sources.title: Musée du Louvre, collection record RF 1158 (the cataloguer's description; our translations)
Henry Lapauze, Ingres, sa vie et son œuvre (Paris, 1911), pp. 159-160 (our translations)
The Courtauld, London, 'Study for La Grande Odalisque', D.1995.XX.1 (label text, 2023)
Charles Blanc, Ingres, sa vie et ses ouvrages (Paris, 1870), pp. 27-28 (our translations)
Lettres à David, sur le Salon de 1819, par quelques élèves de son école (Paris, 1819), pp. 71-72 (our translations)
J.-Y. Maigne, G. Chatellier and H. Norlöff, 'Extra vertebrae in Ingres' La Grande Odalisque', Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine 97 (2004)

c2m.text: Lapauze put it plainly: without her Eastern props, she would be no odalisque.

c2a.text: Titian came up for her pose, not her props.

correction.tempting: In 1819, critics compared her with Titian.
correction.truth: David's pupils said her pose recalled a Titian. The props do another job: they make her 'Eastern'.
correction.evidence: Lettres à David (1819). Lapauze (1911): an odalisque only by her Eastern props. The Courtauld: the props 'orientalised' her.

c2b.text: Yes. For Lapauze (1911) she is an odalisque only through her Eastern props, and owes her name to them. The Courtauld says the turban and props 'orientalised' the subject.

c2c.text: They suggest one, but they're a borrowed decor.

correction.tempting: The title's word, odalisque, means a woman of a harem.
correction.truth: Lapauze called the props a decor borrowed from 'Turkey in Asia'; for the Courtauld, they 'orientalised' the subject.
correction.evidence: Henry Lapauze, Ingres (1911), our translation. The Courtauld, London: label for Ingres's study for the painting (2023).

extends.concept: From 'painted in Rome' and 'it stayed with Ingres in Rome' (level) to the place Ingres wrote on the canvas himself

c1q.what_you_learn: Ingres signed and dated the picture along the lower edge of the mattress, at lower right: 'J.A.Ingres. Pxit 1814.Rom', his name, 1814 and Rome.

c1q.confidence: High: the Louvre record gives the signature's text and position (lower right), and the lettering is legible in the crop ('I A INGRES P[xi]t 1814 ROM'); Delaborde and Lapauze independently give 1814 and Rome. The record's own transcription is quoted as the Louvre's.
c1q.notes: Ledger claims odalisque-002 (signature, Louvre record; POP is the same Louvre data and reads 'Pat' for 'Pxit'), odalisque-005 (our looking: the signature along the lower edge of the mattress at right), odalisque-007, -013, -017. 'Pxit' is not expanded or translated, since no source we read glosses it. The level says she was painted in Rome (n1b) and stayed there (q2); the close-up adds that Ingres wrote the place on the canvas, and the Naples/Paris near misses are real places in the picture's story.

extends.concept: From the title's word, odalisque (level), to what actually makes her one: the Eastern props

c2q.what_you_learn: The fan, the turban and the other props are what make this nude an 'odalisque': Lapauze says she is one only through her Eastern accessories, and the Courtauld that they orientalised the subject.

regionSources.title: Henry Lapauze, Ingres (Paris, 1911), pp. 159-160 (our translation)
regionSources.quote: Ingres, ayant emprunté son décor à la Turquie d'Asie, — avec le narghilé, le tabouret incrusté, le turban, l'éventail, le chapelet d'ambre, — appela sa femme couchée : l'Odalisque. [...] La célèbre figure n'a de l'odalisque que ses accessoires orientaux, et son nom, qu'elle doit à ses accessoires mêmes.
regionSources.supports: Our translation: Ingres, having borrowed his decor from Turkey in Asia (the narghile, the inlaid stool, the turban, the fan, the amber rosary), called his reclining woman the Odalisque. [...] The famous figure has nothing of the odalisque but her oriental accessories, and her name, which she owes to those accessories.
regionSources.readVia: Saved Internet Archive OCR text in the research folder, re-read 16 Oct 2026

c2q.confidence: High for the region (the Louvre record places the peacock-feather fan in her right hand on her bent left leg; Blanc names the feather fan in her hand; the eye-spots are plain in the crop). The reason is two attributed readings that agree (Lapauze 1911, the Courtauld 2023), framed as theirs; neither is Ingres's own statement.
c2q.notes: Ledger claims odalisque-003 (Louvre description), -006 (Lapauze), -040 (Courtauld), -062 (JRSM gloss), -021 (Lettres à David on the pose). Not used: the Courtauld's 'Ingres never travelled outside of Europe' (Courtauld only), Lapauze's 'Venus' remark (Lapauze only), and the Montauban record's report that the bus company thought she held 'something other than a fan' (Montauban only). Crop framed on the hand, fan and leg; it shows no more of the nude than the hand and leg.
